title: Sums of Independent Variables
short: The distribution of X + Y comes from adding over every split: P(X + Y = s) = Σ P(X = k) P(Y = s − k), with an integral for densities.
trouble: Students add the two pmfs or densities instead of convolving them. The sum of two independent uniform variables has a triangular density, not a uniform one.

blocks.html: If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, what is the distribution of $X + Y$? Not the sum of the two distributions: a total can be made in several ways, and we must add over all of them. This uses the independence of random variables and, for densities, integrating out a variable.
For independent $X$ and $Y$: $$P(X + Y = s) = \sum_k P(X = k)\,P(Y = s - k), \qquad f_{X + Y}(s) = \int f_X(t)\,f_Y(s - t)\,dt.$$ This operation is called convolution.

The event $X + Y = s$ splits by the value of $X$: $X = k$ and $Y = s - k$, for each $k$. These pieces are disjoint, so their probabilities add, and independence turns each piece into a product. For densities, the same splitting turns the sum into an integral: slide the flipped density $f_Y(s - t)$ across $f_X(t)$ and measure their overlap.

blocks.cap: Two dice: the grid holds the products of the two pmfs, and the six highlighted cells add to the probability of a total of 7.

blocks.name: prob-convolve
blocks.cap: Two uniform densities on 0 to 1: the overlap of one with the other flipped and slid to s gives the density of the sum, a triangle.

blocks.title: Two dice
blocks.q: Find $P(X + Y = 7)$ for two fair dice, and $P(X + Y = 5)$ for a four-sided die plus a six-sided die.
steps: Two dice: the splits $(1, 6), (2, 5), \ldots, (6, 1)$ each have probability $\frac{1}{36}$: total $\frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$.
Four-sided and six-sided: the splits $(1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1)$ each have probability $\frac{1}{24}$: total $\frac{4}{24} = \frac{1}{6}$.

blocks.title: Two uniforms
blocks.q: $X$ and $Y$ are independent and uniform on $[0, 1]$. Find the density of $S = X + Y$.
steps: $f_S(s) = \int_{0}^{1} f_Y(s - t)\,dt$ is the length of $\{t \in [0, 1]: 0 \le s - t \le 1\}$.
For $0 \le s \le 1$ that set is $[0, s]$: $f_S(s) = s$. For $1 \le s \le 2$ it is $[s - 1, 1]$: $f_S(s) = 2 - s$.
A triangle peaking at $s = 1$: middle totals can be made in more ways.

blocks.title: Two Poisson counts
blocks.q: $X$ and $Y$ are independent Poisson with means $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Show that $X + Y$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda + \mu$.
steps: $$= \frac{e^{-(\lambda + \mu)}}{n!}\sum_{k} \binom{n}{k}\lambda^{k}\mu^{n - k} = e^{-(\lambda + \mu)}\frac{(\lambda + \mu)^{n}}{n!}$$ by the binomial theorem.
blocks.a: Poisson with mean $\lambda + \mu$. (Similarly, binomials with the same $p$ add: $n_1 + n_2$ trials.)

blocks.html: Adding the pmfs or densities instead of convolving them. The "sum" of two uniform densities on $[0, 1]$ would have total area 2, and it would not say anything about totals between 1 and 2. Check: the result must add (or integrate) to 1, and its range must run from the smallest possible total to the largest.
